issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette: Andrew, 35, is a special-education teacher at a public elementary school in a small Midwestern town. On a damp Thursday evening, after closing the last class, he walked the two-block route home. A figure in a dark hoodie stepped out of a parking lot, thrust a hand toward Andrew's pocket, and shouted an obscuring curse. The man's voice was high and sharp, and the sudden pain that shot through Andrew's neck when the robber grabbed his wrist left a lingering ache. The officer on the scene, with badge flashing, spoke calmly but its presence felt like a looming threat. Andrew's heart hammered and he could not stop the images of the robbery from flooding his mind. The shouting and the officer's authority became immediate triggers. As soon as any voice rises above normal volume, Andrew is flooded with the vivid, photographic recall of the night his life felt stolen. The images arrive so clearly he can see the robber's face, feel the weight of the stolen wallet in his hands, and hear the officer's command to "calm down." When these images surface, Andrew is seized by an intense rage at the injustice of it all, followed by a crushing guilt that he should have done more to prevent it. These emotions are not mere fleeting feelings; they are anchored in his sense of inadequacy and a belief that someone else would not have found themselves in such a situation. In this moment, the memory forces him into a state of threat, where he cannot relax, his mind racing, and he scans every room for an exit as if the walls themselves might close in. The terror of the moment has woven itself into a pattern. The flashbacks that strike at the least of disturbances, the feeling of being unable to relax even in a safe environment, and the frantic search for escape routes feed back into his memory. When Andrew's heart rate spikes, his mind immediately pulls back to the night of the robbery, creating a vicious cycle. The hypervigilance that has become his constant companion now fuels the negative appraisal of his own inadequacy; each pause in his breathing feels like a sign that he is still in danger, and he concludes that he has failed to protect himself or the children he teaches. In turn, that appraisal sharpens his threat response: the more he doubts his strength, the more he believes he is doomed to repeat that moment. The threat of sudden danger makes the mere sound of someone shouting a new trigger; the slightest raised voice is enough to pull him back into the image of the hooded man and the officer's stern gaze. This loop has taken a toll on his work life. Andrew began arriving early to prepare lesson plans, refusing to leave the classroom when students were still in the building because he could not be sure that the hallway would not become a trap. He now carries a notebook with a list of "exits" for every hallway and hallway, and often spends hours in the staff lounge, pacing and listening to the murmurs of colleagues as if they might be warning him of unseen danger. His colleagues notice that his enthusiasm has waned; the once vibrant lessons now feel routine and devoid of the joy he once found in helping children with learning differences. At home, he has stopped returning calls from friends, preferring to stay in his bedroom where he believes he is safest. The cumulative weight of these experiences has finally led Andrew to seek therapy. He fears that if he cannot break the cycle, he may lose his job, his ability to support his modest income, and his sense of identity as a caring educator. Yet he also holds a fragile hope that, with help, he can reclaim the calm he once found in the classroom and the confidence he once believed he possessed. He is ready to confront the triggers, but he does not know if he will ever feel relaxed again.
